OBJECTIVES:

                      OBJECTIVES:


                                                    By the end of this lecture students should be able to describe:
                                                               ◼  Surface anatomy of the lungs
                                                               ◼  Pleura and pleural cavity
                                                               ◼  Clinical cases:
                                           ◼Open pneumothorax
                                                                  ◼Pleuritis and thoracentesis





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pneumothorax: Air in pleural cavity resulting in collapse of lungs
Pleuritis: Inflammation of pleural cavity (due to edema) resulting in inflammatory
fluid production
Normal: Serous fluid in pleural cavity is constantly being secreted and reabsorbed by
mesothelium of pleura

Surface anatomy of the lungs
                          Surface anatomy of the lungs




                                                                      Apex of the lungs
                                                                                                  ◼    projects into the neck 2.5
                                                                     cm above of the clavicle

                                                                                            Inferior border of the lungs
                                                                                                  ◼    follows a curving line,
                                                                                          which crosses:
                                                                                                  ◼   6th rib at the MCL
                                                                                                  ◼   8th rib at the MAL
                                                                                                  ◼   10th rib at the scapular
                                                                                                                         line

                                                            10        6
                                                                 8





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

This is the inferior border of the right lung (3 lobes, 2 fissures). Pleura go much
deeper than inferior border.
Blue line: lower border of pleural cavity
Other line: lower border of lung
Between both: costal diaphragmatic recess, which is the deepness in the pleural
cavity with the most serous fluid.
Lobes:
1. Mid-clavicular line (MCL): vertical line down the clavicle (6th rib)
2. Mid-axillary line (MAL): vertical line in the middle of axillary cavity (8th rib)
3. Scapular: vertical line on lower end of scapula (10th rib)

                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Penetrated stab wounds:
1. Thoracic cavity: Knife typically goes between ribs. Depending on where the knife
goes, a specific lobe of the lungs will be affected.
2. Front right side at midclavicular line between ribs 2 and 3: Superior lobe affected.
3. Front left side at midclavicular line between ribs 2 and 3: Heart will be affected
instead of lungs (right ventricle)
4. Lower border of sternum: Right atrium is affected because heart is rotated.
5. Apex: left lung

                                                                                                        8

PLEURA

                      PLEURA

                                                                                   The pleura is the serous
                                                                            membrane that invest the
                                                                                                lungs in the lateral
                                                                                      compartments of the
                                                                                                        thoracic cavity
                                                                                            Parietal Pleura
                                                                                                    ◼    Cervical pleura
                                                                                                    ◼    Costal pleura
                                                                                                    ◼   Diaphragmatic pleura
                                                                                                    ◼    Mediastinal pleura





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pleura: serous membrane
Visceral pleura: covers surface of lung
Parietal pleura: covers thorax from inside
Visceral and parietal pleura are interconnected.

(Doctor goes to slide 10 of the Lungs Anatomy Lecture)
The blue line at the bottom is the connection. It covers the hylum of the lungs and
then goes to the thoracic wall where it becomes pleura.

(Doctor goes to slide 13 of this lecture)





                                                                                                        9

A classical representation of this is the air balloon (pink). If you put your fist in the balloon
(not strongly), the fist will be like a lung and the balloon will be like pleura
(interconnection). Instead of air in the balloon we have serous fluid. The connection is
underneath the hylum

Parietal pleura is subdivided into:
1. Cervical pleura: Covers tops of lungs above the clavicle (in neck)
2. Costal pleura: Covers internal surface of ribs
3. Diaphragmatic pleura: Covers diaphragm on top
4. Mediastinal pleura: Covers mediastinal structures of rib.





                                                                                                           9

PLEURA

                      PLEURA

                                                                                            Visceral pleura
                                                                                                    ◼   completely covers the
                                                                                            external surfaces of
                                                                                                   the lungs and extends
                                                                                                                to the depths of the
                                                                                                                    fissures





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Visceral pleura completely covers the external surfaces of lungs and extends to the
depths of fissures, which split the lobes in the lung (goes inside)





                                                                                                      10

Parietal Visceral Pleura

                               Parietal & Visceral Pleura





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

The video shows a fresh dissection. The lungs are grayish because they belong to a
smoker.
Visceral pleura: layer that covers the lung
Parietal pleura: layer that binds the cavity
Both layers are continuous with each other here around the hylum of the lung.
Pleural cavity: space between visceral and parietal pleura containing serous fluid.





                                                                                                      11

Pleural cavity

                            Pleural cavity

                                                                                                ◼  The pleural cavity is the
                                                                                                         potential space between the
                                                                                                              parietal and visceral layers of
                                                                                              the pleura.
                                                                                                ◼  Normally contains a small
                                                                                amount of serous fluid to
                                                                                                   allow the two layers to move on
                                                                                       each other with the minimum
                                                                                                                         friction.





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Cohesion/Adhesion/Tension: Force which keeps two glasses together if fluid is
dropped in between them. We hold one glass and the other one will stay in the
same place because of the fluid in between. If we put something in between (like a
knife) and disconnect them, they fall apart. Removing the fluid from the pleural
cavity will cause the lung to fall apart from the inner surface of the thorax. Lungs
have elastic property and follow the thoracic wall movement because of this
adhesion only. Removing this force results in lungs collapsing, which happens if air
enters. This is pneumothorax. This air can come from anywhere (lungs, bronchi, or
stabbing wounds).





                                                                                                      12

Costodiaphragmatic recess

                          Costodiaphragmatic recess

                                                                                                ◼  In deep inspiration, areas of
                                                                                                    apposition separate to allow
                                                                                room for lung expansion in the
                                                                                                          pleural recesses:
                                                                                  costodiaphragmatic recess
                                                                                              corresponds to the distance
                                                                                    between the lower border of
                                                                                               the lung and the lower border
                                                                                                              of the pleura





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

There is only 1 cm in between parietal and visceral plura. The real space between
them cannot be seen (too small since they are stuck together)
Costodiaphragmatic recess: Place where all serous fluid sits in. The diaphragm is
dome shaped, so the lung is not completely at this lower angle. It sits at the level of
rib 6, and the pleura is sitting below. So if we need to get a sample of the fluid for a
test, we collect it from the costodiaphragmatic recess.





                                                                                                      13

Open pneumothorax

                      Open pneumothorax

                                                                                      ◼    It is the entry of air into a pleural
                                                                                  cavity causing lung collapse.
                                                                                      ◼  Open pneumothorax – due to stab
                                                                         wounds of the thoracic wall which
                                                                                             pierce the parietal pleura so that the
                                                                                 pleural cavity is open to the
                                                                             outside air via the lung or through the
                                                                                       chest wall.
                                                                                      ◼   Air moves freely through the wound
                                                                                         during inspiration and expiration.
                                                                                      During inspiration, air enters the
                                                                                       chest wall, and the mediastinum will
                                                                                                               shift toward the other side and
                                                                              compress the opposite lung. During
                                                                                   expiration, air exits the wound, and
                                                                                      the mediastinum moves back toward
                                                                                      the affected side.



                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

In open pneumothorax, the collapsed lung will sit close to the root of the lung
because it holds the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, and two pulmonary veins
(fixed). Everything else is movable. Now we have a huge cavity (space) between the
visceral and parietal pleura which is not okay. Because of gravity, all fluid will go
down into the costodiaphragmatic recess, so there is no fluid between the parietal
and visceral plura, and air takes this space.
X-ray of open pneumothorax:
Left side: normal (grayish lung tissue)
Right side: Collapsed lung near the root of the lung. It looks black because air is
inside, and air looks black on X-ray films (patient is alive because of other lung).





                                                                                                      14

Open pneumothorax: a hole which air can go through. In the affected side, air will go in
and out from the pleural cavity (instead of lungs).
Treatment:
1.  First seal the hole
2. Then remove air using a syringe (actively). After most of the air is removed, the rest will
   be extracted on its own with time (passively).





                                                                                                          14

Nerve supply of the pleura
                        Nerve supply of the pleura




                                                   Parietal Pleura – sensitive to
                                                        general sensibilities (pain,
                                                       temperature, touch, and
                                                         pressure) - somatic sensory
                                                    innervation:
                                                       ◼  costal pleura – intercostal
                                               nerves
                                                       ◼  mediastinal pleura – phrenic
                                               nerve
                                                       ◼  diaphragmatic pleura –
                                                         phrenic nerve over the domes
                                               and lower 6 intercostal nerves
                                                   around the periphery





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Parietal means walls of the body, which belong to the soma. The body is divided into
soma (body) and viscera (internal organs). Whatever is left when we remove internal
organs is soma. You can feel soma, but not viscera (almost true, because you can
feel pain in the stomach but it’s different). All internal organs have smooth muscles
in the walls.

Internal organs have three layers:
1. Inner: Mucous
2. Middle: Muscularis
3. Outer: Serous/adventitia





                                                                                                      15

The heart has cardiac muscle made of myocardium. Skeletal muscles can be controlled, but
muscles of the stomach, esophagus, and heart cannot be controlled (autonomic nervous
system). Costal pleura belongs to the soma. We have the sensory component, which will be
covered by somatic intercostal nerves below every rib. Ribs and muscles in between belong
to the body (somatic). Phrenic nerve is somatic and sits at/supplies the diaphragm, which is
skeletal muscle (voluntary). Apart from motor components, nerves also have sensory
components which arise from sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia. Sensations in the
soma can be localized (when you pinch yourself, you know where the pain came from). If
something happened to the internal organs, the patient will feel the pain, but it is visceral
(not localized, you cannot point where it is coming from). The only organ which has no pain
at all is the brain (surgery can be done without anesthesia). Pleura will have sensation and
somatic pain. In pneumonia (Inflammation of lungs), the patient will have discomfort and
cough but will not know where it’s coming from due to visceral pleura.





                                                                                                          15

Nerve supply of the pleura
                        Nerve supply of the pleura




                                                     Visceral Pleura – sensitive to
                                                                 stretch but insensitive to
                                                           general sensibilities;
                                               autonomic nerve supply
                                                      from the pulmonary plexus





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Visceral pleura belongs to the pulmonary system and is sensitive to stretch.





                                                                                                      16

Answer: A
Thoracocentesis: Inserting a syringe needle through the thoracic wall into the
thoracic cavity through the parietal pleura to extract something (air/ fluid), which
leads to painful sensation and nausea. Phrenic nerve runs in front of bronchi
between mediastinal pleura and mediastinum. This procedure is done between the
ribs (intercostal nerves) and not the sternum.





                                                                                                      17

Borders of the pleural cavity

                          Borders of the pleural cavity

                                                                                    ◼    1. Cervical pleura may be affected in
                                                                                   case of improper subclavian
                                                                            venipuncture.

                                                                                    ◼    2. Costodiaphragmatic recess is
                                                                                 deepest place in the pleural cavity, around
                                                                                    the chest wall, there are two rib
                                                                             interspaces separating the inferior limit
                                                                                                  of parietal pleural reflections from the
                                                                                                        inferior border of the lungs and visceral
                                                                                            pleura:
                                                                     2           1.   Midclavicular line - between ribs 6-8
                                                                                                                                 2.   Midaxillary line - between ribs 8-10
                                                                                                                                3.   Paravertebral line between ribs 10-12





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pink structure: lung and its lower borders (6, 8, and 10)
Blue structure: costodiaphragmatic recess
Pleural cavity: ends below border of lungs.
Midclavicular line: pleural cavity at rib 8 and below it rib 10.
Scapular line: 12th rib

Between the lower border of the lung and lower border of the pleural cavity we
always have two ribs. If you only remember rib 6, 2 ribs above will be a horizontal
fissure and 2 ribs below will be the lower border of the pleural cavity





                                                                                                      18

Pleuritis (pleurisy)

                               Pleuritis (pleurisy)



                                                                                     ◼    It is inflammation of the pleura
                                                                               which can lead to pleural
                                                                            adhesions. Rough surfaces rub
                                                                                        together and can be heard with a
                                                                                     stethoscope (pleural friction
                                                                                    rub).
                                                                                     ◼   Level of the inflammatory fluid is
                                                                                             well visible on X-ray.





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pleuritis:
-  Inflammation of pleura due to pneumonia.
-  Most likely bacterial because if it is not treated properly, it destroys the lung
   tissue.
-  Once it gets close to the external surface of the lungs, it will involve the pleura
  membrane (visceral pleura).
-   It is associated with secretion of plenty of serous inflammatory fluid, which is
  what is seen in this x-ray film. Air looks dark in x-ray films and fluid is a white
   straight horizontal line.
-  Air starts building up from the top and fluid from the bottom.





                                                                                                      19

-  Costodiaphragmatic recess will be filled, go up, and compress the lungs.
-   Pleuritis causes problems with breathing because lungs will not be collapsed, they will
  be compressed from the bottom by the fluid since you cannot compress fluid.
-   It also causes pleural friction or rupture, so when you auscultate, you hear a sound.





                                                                                                          19

Pleuritic pain

                               Pleuritic pain


                                                                                        ◼    Pleurisy causes sharp chest pain
                                                                                                           (pleuritic pain) that worsens during
                                                                                              breathing.
                                                                                        ◼   Inflammation of the costal pleura
                                                                                    produces local pain in the chest
                                                                                                wall via the intercostal nerves.
                                                                                        ◼    Irritation of mediastinal pleura
                                                                                    produces referred pain via the
                                                                              phrenic nerve to the shoulder
                                                                            dermatomes of C3-5.





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Pneumonia: typically painless because lungs are internal organs, so the exact
location cannot be pointed.
Pleuritis: painful because parietal pleura and intercostal nerves provide pain. It can
also affect the phrenic nerve (somatic from C3 to C5), which causes referred
shoulder pain in the dermatomes associated with the same dorsal root ganglia
supplying internal organs. In the dorsal root ganglia we have sensory neurons for the
skin. Dermatome is the area of the skin which gets innervated from one dorsal root
ganglia. Another group of neurons supplies internal organs, so pain radiates from
there to the same dorsal root ganglia (felt in dermatome). Other nerves also supply
the shoulder. Referred pain is on the same side as affected lung (ipsilateral)





                                                                                                      20

Thoracentesis

                           Thoracentesis


                                                                                               ◼    It is the insertion of a needle
                                                                                                             into the pleural cavity to
                                                                                   remove air, blood, or other
                                                                                                                       fluids
                                                                                               ◼    Usually done in the 7 - 9th ICS
                                                              MAL 1-2 ICS below fluid level
                                                                                                                  (for fluids or fluids and air) or
                                                                                                           at the 2nd ICS MCL (for air
                                                                                                    alone)
                                                                                               ◼   Needle is inserted in an
                                                                                             intercostal space close to the
                                                                            upper border of the rib below
                                                                                                          to avoid injury to the main
                                                                                                             intercostal neurovascular
                                                                                            bundle





                                         @ Dr. Olena, 2026

Patient posture:
1.  Sitting down: fluid will go down due to gravity, making it easier to do the
   procedure
2.  Leaning to the front: makes spaces between ribs a little wider
Steps:
1. Localize the point of procedure and inject local anesthetics (bupivicaine/lidocaine)
with a small syringe and wait for the effect.
2. Pass the needle of the syringe through the skin, subcutaneous tissue, intercostal
muscles, pleural, until you get into costodiaphragmatic recess of pleural cavity to
withdraw fluid.





                                                                                                      21

This syringe is not the same as the one for intramuscular injections, the needle is bigger
and wider (thick middle). Once the inflammatory fluid is withdrawn and the lung will not be
compressed, the patient will feel immediate relief. We target 7 to 9 intercostal spaces in the
mid-axillary line because that is the widest place between the ribs. We do not go above
these ribs because there is a chance to damage the lower border of the lung. We do not go
below these ribs so we do not miss the pleural cavity (can accidentally go to the liver on the
right side)

In pneumothorax, unlike the fluid, air tends to collect up, so we cannot do
thoracocentesis. We do it in the opposite location and remove air from the top of the
pleural cavity (not bottom). This is done at the second intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
(under the clavicle). The needle is inserted on top, underneath the rib (intercostal space) so
we don't hit the nerve below the rib. So thoracocentesis is done above the rib at the lower
or middle rib.





                                                                                                          21

Answer: D
Pleural effusion: too much fluid in the pleural cavity (in pleuritis)
The lung is sitting on the level of rib 6, so 8 to 10 will be the safe spot (so we don’t
punch the lung).
